items.title: PIX2DB: Reconstructing Executable Relational Databases from Document Images with a 2B Vision-Language Model
items.summary: Abstract Tables trapped in screenshots, scans, receipts and charts are usually extracted as markup that keeps the layout but not the relational meaning: merged cells stay merged, an invoice header and its line items stay unrelated, and “$1,250.00” stays a string. We study image-to-database reconstruction: given one image, produce a SQLite dump whose schema, column types, keys and rows load and can be queried as they are. Training data with exact gold databases is obtained in two ways: by rendering samples of the Spider databases at six layout levels, and by converting PubTabNet, FinTabNet and CORD annotations under the same normalization rules. A 2B model (Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA) trained on 36,589 pairs and followed by a deterministic verify-and-repair layer reaches 0.86 table exact match and 0.99 foreign-key recall on rendered tables from unseen databases, against 0.75/0.75 for the 8B model of the same family prompted for SQL and 0.47/0.00 for an 8B HTML-to-SQLite pipeline. On held-out real images it obtains cell F1 0.81 (PubTabNet) and 0.96 (FinTabNet) and recall 0.93 on CORD receipt photos. On TabRecSet, a source not used in training, it is the best system that writes a database directly (0.52) but trails the 8B HTML pipeline (0.58), mostly in reading text from photographs. items.title: Differential diagnosis of pulmonary Talaromyces marneffei infection and pulmonary tuberculosis in HIV/AIDS patients using a CT-based multimodal 2.5D deep learning approach
items.summary: Background To investigate the diagnostic value of a computed tomography (CT)-based multimodal 2.5-dimensional (2.5D) deep learning model for differentiating Talaromyces marneffei (TSM) from pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) in patients with human immunodeficiency virus infection/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (HIV/AIDS). Methods A total of 380 HIV/AIDS patients with pulmonary infections who were admitted to the Fourth People’s Hospital of Nanning from January 2018 to August 2025 were retrospectively enrolled, including 203 patients with PTB, 177 with TSM. The cohort was randomly divided into a training set and a test set at a ratio of 7:3. A clinical model, a radiomics model, and a 2.5D deep learning model were constructed separately. Results In the clinical feature model, Random Forest achieved the optimal performance, with a test set AUC of 0.856. In the radiomics model, XGBoost attained the highest AUC of 0.866. In the 2.5D deep learning model, ResNet18 performed best at the slice level with an AUC of 0.865, and the patient-level support vector machine (SVM) model based on MIL achieved an AUC of 0.885. The multimodal combined model integrating clinical, radiomics, and deep learning features achieved the highest AUC of 0.931 and a specificity of 0.981. items.title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
items.summary: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. items.title: Gate3DGen: A Pre-processing Model that Selectively Purifies Real-World Images for 3D Generation
items.summary: Single-image 3D generation has achieved high fidelity on curated benchmarks, yet degrades sharply on real-world images with uneven illumination, blur, and occlusions. Purifying such inputs requires deciding when to intervene and preserving the visual cues needed for 3D generation, while leaving clean inputs unchanged. We introduce Gate3DGen, a selective pre-processing model that gates image inputs to existing 3D generators without retraining them. A degradation-aware router bypasses inputs classified as clean and extracts features to guide purification of the remaining inputs. Conditioned on these features, a 3D-oriented one-step purifier purifies degraded inputs with spatial losses that encourage preservation of object identity, contours, and textural cues. To provide paired supervision, we construct a synthetic data engine that renders clean views of 3D assets and synthesises composite degradations. On the synthetic benchmark, the purifier improves image fidelity and downstream 3D geometry in only 2.3s on average, reducing TRELLIS.2 mesh distance by 61.5% relative to degraded inputs. VLM evaluation and human preferences on real photographs further support identity preservation and degradation correction. More demos and code are available at https://supra-3d.github.io/gate3dgen.

items.title: OmniRay: Camera-Agnostic Monocular 3D Reconstruction with Composite Ray Fields
items.summary: Monocular models recover 3D geometry from a single image in one pass, but most assume a pinhole camera and produce distorted geometry on the wide-angle imagery produced by fisheye and panoramic lenses. Camera-aware models remove this assumption by predicting a per-pixel ray field. However, they represent different camera geometries using a single fixed basis to capture both the overall camera projection and its finer variations. We argue that camera geometry can be viewed as having a hierarchy of complexity for representing rays. We present OmniRay, a feed-forward model whose Ray Module is composed of three components: a monotone radial base that captures radially symmetric structure, a spherical-harmonic residual for smooth deviations from it, and a free-form residual for remaining local variation. These components are composed as successive rotations on the sphere, allowing the representation to accommodate diverse camera geometries. Given a single image, OmniRay predicts a ray direction and an up-to-scale radial distance for every pixel, from which a 3D point cloud is recovered without needing camera information at inference time. Extensive experiments across different camera configurations demonstrate that OmniRay establishes a new state-of-the-art in camera-agnostic monocular 3D reconstruction.

items.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
items.summary: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

items.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
items.summary: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. items.title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
items.summary: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.

items.title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
items.summary: We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold. First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force. Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole"). We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments. We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learni

items.title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
items.summary: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality

items.title: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models
items.summary: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less t

items.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
items.summary: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. Our fix eliminates the previously-observed "Slingshot" phenomenon, speeds up grokking with weight decay, prevents accuracy collapse without weight decay, stops student networks from drifting away from the teacher during distillation, and shows that after memorization, logit growth is bounded by an equilibrium between weight decay and Adam's $ε$ hyperparameter.

items.title: Neuromorphic Computing Architectures for Low-Power Edge Inference in IoT Applications
items.summary: The blistering advancements witnessed in the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem have led to the urgency of search outcomes that provide energy efficient, low latency, and smart processing support that manifests itself right at the edge. The traditional edge computing devices built on von Neumann architecture are inherently limited by being optimized to be adjacent in memory and processing components, which results in the high power required and latency, which are highly undesirable in devices with limited power resources; wearables, smart sensors, and remote-monitoring systems. A Neuromorphic computing approach based on the human brain blueprint presents a better alternative due to its implementation of spiking neural networks (SNNs) that allow asynchronous and event-driven computation, thus dramatically lowering power demand and yet being able to run real-time inference. This paper includes a holistic comparison of the most recent examples of the neuromorphic hardware platforms, such as Intel Loihi, IBM TrueNorth, and BrainScaleS system, with regard to their learning architectures, energy consumption, throughput, and suitability to the edge-based IoT applications. An empirical case study is carried out, which is a keyword spotting case study and event-based gesture recognition case study using Google Speech Commands and the DVS Gesture dataset sets, respectively. items.title: Spiking neural network inference on FPGAs with hls4ml
items.summary: Abstract Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) provide a naturally temporal machinelearning framework. Their neurons maintain an internal state and propagate information through discrete spikes, enabling low-latency temporal inference. Although SNNs are often associated with asynchronous neuromorphic processors, many scientific real-time inference systems rely on conventional synchronous fieldprogrammable gate arrays (FPGAs) and high-level synthesis (HLS) workflows. In this paper we present an extension of hls4ml that enables clock-driven deployment of SNNs trained in PyTorch onto FPGA firmware. We demonstrate the workflow using a dense quantised SNN trained on the Heidelberg Spiking Digits dataset where it achieves inference latencies of approximately 34µs. We validate the generated design through software reference comparisons, HLS C simulation, HLS synthesis, export, and Vivado synthesis reports. This work opens up the hls4ml toolkit to neuromorphic computing, allowing streamlined optimisation, synthesis, and deployment of SNN models for realtime inference.

items.title: SEPhIA: spiking electro-photonic integrated tiled architecture leveraging multi-wavelength lasers for scalable optical neuromorphic computing
items.summary: Abstract Research into optical spiking neural networks (SNNs) has primarily focused on spiking devices, networks of excitable lasers or numerical modeling of large architectures, often overlooking key constraints such as limited optical power, crosstalk and footprint. We introduce SEPhIA, a photonic-electronic, multi-tiled SNN architecture emphasizing implementation feasibility and realistic scaling. SEPhIA leverages microring modulators (MRMs) and multi-wavelength sources to achieve effective $$ < 1$$ < 1 laser-per-spiking neuron ratio. We validate SEPhIA at both device and architecture levels by time‑domain co‑simulating excitable CMOS‑MRM coupled circuits and by devising a physics‑aware, trainable optoelectronic SNN model, with both approaches utilizing experimentally derived device parameters. The multi-layer optoelectronic SNN achieves classification accuracies over 90% on a four-class spike-encoded dataset, closely comparable to software models. A design space study further quantifies how photonic device parameters impact SNN performance under constrained signal-to-noise conditions. SEPhIA offers a scalable, expressive, physically grounded solution for neuromorphic photonic computing, capable of addressing spike-encoded tasks.

items.title: The Environmental Impacts of Language Model Training Keep Rising Now is the Time to Catch Impacts on the Rebound
items.summary: Recent Machine Learning (ML) approaches have shown increased performance on benchmarks at the cost of escalating compute demands. Hardware, algorithmic and carbon optimizations have been proposed to curb energy use and environmental impacts. We estimate the environmental impacts associated with training models documented in the Epoch AI database over the last decade, with a particular focus on impacts associated with Large Language Models and the hardware used to train them. We find that energy use and environmental impacts associated with training ML models have increased exponentially, even when considering impact reduction strategies such as using less carbon intensive electricity mixes or more efficient hardware. Optimization strategies do not mitigate the impacts induced by model training, suggesting rebound effect. We show that the impacts of hardware mustbe considered over the entire life cycle rather than the sole use phase in order to avoid impact shifting. Our study demonstrates that increasing efficiency alone does not ensure sustainability. There is an urgent need to systematically integrate environmental impacts in NLP evaluation practices to better inform the community and support the use of impact as a feature in research planning and decision making.

items.title: Are Benchmarks a source of bias in LLMs? MMLU, CommonSenseQA and MGSM under the Microscope
items.summary: Evaluation is an essential process in the development and use of NLP systems. Benchmarks are widely used to calibrate systems, determine the efficiency of techniques, but also to advertise recently launched language models. Not only do benchmarks allow for evaluation and system comparisons, but they are also commonly utilized as training and validation corpora. In this paper, we aim at characterizing the "world knowledge" that is put forth by benchmarks by closely inspecting their content. Through qualitative manual annotations (+15k instances) as well as quantitative automatic analyses, we uncover the presence of both explicit and implicit biases in MMLU, Common-SenseQA and MGSM, ranging from representational imbalance to bluntly sexist and racist instances. Our findings demonstrate that current NLP evaluation practices pose numerous quality issues, reinforce stereotypes and even contain explicitly harmful content. The current operationalization of benchmarks is questioned, and we provide recommendations and directions for further ethical evaluation.

items.title: Helping the Helper: LLM-Assisted Problem Articulation for Older Adults Seeking Technology Support
items.summary: Older adults often struggle to articulate technology support needs due to unfamiliar technical terminology and age-related cognitive changes. We explore how large language models (LLMs) can facilitate this problem articulation process. Through a diary study (n = 27), we identified four communication barriers in older adults’ queries: verbosity, incompleteness, over-specification, and under-specification. To mitigate these, we developed an LLM pipeline that clarifies context and paraphrases unstructured queries. LLM-rephrased queries significantly improved automated solution accuracy (69% vs. 35%). Furthermore, younger adults (n = 48) acting as technology helpers understood LLM-rephrased queries better (93.7% vs. 65.8%) and reported greater ease in providing support. Older adults (n = 34) also found the resulting solutions highly actionable (94.7%). Finally, we contribute the first synthetic dataset of older adults’ technology assistance queries (STAQ). This work demonstrates how LLMs can improve technology support seeking for older adults by addressing age-related communication barriers.

items.title: Physical AI Bridging the Digital Mind and the Material World
items.summary: Physical AI is a pivotal moment in the interaction of machines with the physical world. It refers to a family of AI systems that interact with the physical world by integrating high-level models with sensors, actuators and control systems to perceive, reason, decide and act in the physical world. Physical AI, unlike generative or digital-only AI, that creates text, code or images within the confines of software, exists where what matters is measurable in motion, force and matter. This article discusses the field in six dimensions historical background in robotics and embodied cognition, underlying architecture of perception, planning and action, industries being reshaped, barriers that continue to limit the field, and engineering and policy reactions that are beginning to take shape, and paths that are likely to shape the next decade. The analysis is based on the latest research in the industry, market forecasts and peer-reviewed studies to ensure a balance between caution and enthusiasm. Results indicate that as Physical AI is making strides in sectors such as transportation, manufacturing, healthcare, and retail, there are still hurdles, including challenges in simulation to reality, energy consumption, ethical considerations, and workforce adaptation. items.title: Triboelectric Nanogenerators for Human‐Robot Motion Energy Harvesting and Sensing: Structures, Embodied Artificial Intelligence, and Self‐Powered Applications
items.summary: ABSTRACT The rapid development of humanoid robots and embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) is accelerating the transformation of elderly care and rehabilitation toward interactive, adaptive, and personalized human–robot collaboration. In this context, motion sensing technology is of critical importance. Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), which convert biomechanical motions into electrical signals, offer a promising route toward self‐powered motion perception in embodied healthcare. This review summarizes recent advances in TENG‐based multimodal motion sensing for human–robot interaction, covering inertial vibration sensing, tactile sensing, non‐contact sensing, continuous trajectory sensing, and joint rotation sensing. The influences of structural configuration, motion mode, sensing direction, detection range, sensitivity, resolution, electrical output, and channel number on sensing performance under specific application scenarios are analyzed. Particular attention is paid to how TENG design strategies influence sensing universality, signal effectiveness, and the reliability of health monitoring and rehabilitation evaluation. Furthermore, the integration of TENGs with artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, including multimodal fusion, network architectures, edge computing, transfer learning, and large language models, is reviewed. items.title: Physical Educational AI (PEAI) A Framework for Action-Centered Intelligence in Education
items.summary: Artificial intelligence in education has traditionally emphasized computational processes such as knowledge representation, automated assessment, personalized feedback, conversational tutoring, and content generation. Recent advances in robotics, multimodal foundation models, and vision-language-action systems have expanded the possibility of connecting artificial intelligence with physical environments. However, the ability to perceive an educational environment or possess an embodied form does not necessarily mean that an AI system can reliably execute educational tasks under physical constraints. Educational environments involve moving students, manipulable objects, limited space, uncertain environmental conditions, safety requirements, time-sensitive interactions, and the possibility of action failure. This paper introduces and formally defines Physical Educational AI (PEAI) as a research framework for artificial intelligence systems that pursue educational objectives through physically grounded execution, real-time control, environmental feedback, and constraint-aware adaptation. PEAI emphasizes not only what an AI system understands or recommends, but also what it physically accomplishes, how it controls the execution process, and whether the resulting physical state satisfies the intended educational objective. items.title: Algorithms For Pre-Processing And Noise Filtering In Streaming Telemetry Data Of Iot Devices
items.summary: This article examines algorithms for preprocessing and filtering noise in streaming telemetry data from IoT devices. We classify noise sources (measurement noise, ADC quantization, and impulse noise during packet loss and retransmission) and formulate requirements for online processing: limited memory, on-the-fly processing without re-passing the data, and predictable computational complexity per sample. We consider moving averages, exponential smoothing, median filters, Hampel filters, recursive Kalman filters, and wavelet noise suppression, as well as hybrid pipelines that combine outlier removal with subsequent smoothing. Using a synthetic telemetry stream simulating temperature sensor readings with Gaussian noise and impulse spikes, we compare the methods in terms of root mean square error (RMSE), processing time per sample, and response latency. The hybrid Hampel filter + exponential smoothing pipeline is shown to reduce RMSE by 84.1% while maintaining O(1) computational complexity per sample, making it suitable for deployment on low-power edge devices.

items.title: Experimental Validation of a Zero-Trust-Based Layered Cybersecurity and Hardening Framework for Smart Metering and IoT Modem Infrastructures
items.summary: Smart meters and Internet of Things (IoT) modems are now essential for remote monitoring and management in energy distribution systems, but they also widen the attack surface. Vulnerabilities span the hardware, firmware, communication, and data-management layers, and this study addresses them with a five-layer security and hardening framework based on the zero-trust model. Seven mechanisms are integrated within a single architecture: endpoint hardware protection, secure boot, mutual authentication, network micro-segmentation, operational command verification, artificial intelligence-based anomaly detection, and privacy-preserving data aggregation. The framework was evaluated in a laboratory testbed across eight scenarios: physical tampering, malicious firmware, unauthorized connection, network scanning, denial-of-service, replay attacks, low-rate stealthy network anomalies, and consumer profiling via data exposure. Cryptographic key zeroization had a mean latency of 14.2 ± 1.1 ms, unauthorized network traffic was blocked according to the configured security policies, and the SIEM alert associated with replay rejection was generated within 127.08 ms. The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based time-series model achieved 95.73% accuracy with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9696. items.title: A Low-Cost IoT Smart Pill Box with Physical Intake Verification: Design and Evaluation in Real-Life Use
items.summary: Medication non-adherence undermines the treatment of chronic diseases, and reminder applications cannot show whether a dose was taken. This paper reports a 52-day field evaluation of a low-cost smart pill box that registers each intake event with an infrared sensor and a reed switch, time-stamps it with a battery-backed clock, queues events locally during network outages and forwards them to a Laravel server that alerts the patient, a caregiver and a physician by staged e-mails. One user with multiple sclerosis, who is also an author, used the device with three scheduled doses per day. Of 155 planned doses, 90 were taken (58.1%); excluding an 8-day period in which the device was deliberately switched off, adherence was 68.7% (95% CI 59–78%) and differed between phases (83.3%, 47.6% and 73.2%). Taken doses were registered at a median deviation of 0 min, 94.4% within five minutes of the alarm; e-mail reminders were followed by intake in 4 of 69 cases. All 90 events recorded after installation matched a planned dose, all 103 device packets were consistent with the database, the median device-to-server delay was 2 s, and the notification chain fired at its thresholds in every case. Deep sleep extended the runtime on a 10,000 mAh power bank by 2.6-fold (from 14 h to 36 h). The sensors register intake events but do not verify ingestion. items.title: Using digital twins as a shared information model for secure software lifecycle management in IoT
items.summary: Secure software updates are essential for maintaining Internet of Things (IoT) systems throughout their operational lifetime. However, software lifecycle information is typically fragmented across software repositories, deployment services, device management platforms, and runtime monitoring systems, limiting interoperability and end-to-end lifecycle visibility. This paper proposes a Digital Twin (DT)-based information model that uses the DT of each device as a shared information contract throughout the operational stages of the IoT secure software update lifecycle. The proposed model extends the DT with software lifecycle information, enabling deployment intentions, installation status, verification results, and runtime observations to be exchanged through a shared representation across heterogeneous software management components. The approach is realised as an extension of Eclipse Ditto and evaluated in a laboratory set-up for telemedicine gateways that combines a real gateway with fleets of emulated devices. A real security update could be followed revision by revision in the gateway’s DT; queries over the DTs identified vulnerable, updated and failed devices correctly, despite injected installation and verification failures and temporarily offline devices; and new lifecycle information and an additional lifecycle component were introduced without changing the existing ones
